q: Composition stoichiometry describes the quantitative relationships among elements in compounds.
e: True. Composition stoichiometry describes the quantitative relationships among elements in compounds. Stoichiometry is the quantitative bookkeeping of how much of each substance takes part in a reaction.

q: In stoichiometric calculation, the SI unit for the amount of chemical substances is the gram.
e: False. The SI basic unit for amount of substance is the mole, with the symbol mol. In stoichiometric calculation, the SI unit for the amount of chemical substances is the gram.

q: One mole of a substance is defined as the amount of substance that contains the same number of particles as there are atoms in exactly 12 g of pure carbon-12.
e: True. One mole of a substance is defined as the amount of substance that contains the same number of particles as there are atoms in exactly 12 g of pure carbon-12. The SI base unit for amount of substance is the mole. One mole is the amount that holds as many particles as 12 g of carbon-12, which is 6.02 x 10^23 particles.

q: One mole of a substance is defined as the amount of substance that contains the same number of particles as there are atoms in exactly 12 g of pure carbon-14.
e: False. One mole of a substance is defined as the amount of substance that contains the same number of particles as there are atoms in exactly 12 g of pure carbon-12. The SI base unit for amount of substance is the mole. One mole is the amount that holds as many particles as 12 g of carbon-12, which is 6.02 x 10^23 particles.

q: One mole is equal to $6.02214179 \times 10^{23}$ particles.
e: True. One mole is equal to 6.02214179 x 10^23 particles. One mole is the amount that holds as many particles as 12 g of carbon-12, which is 6.02 x 10^23 particles.

q: Avogadro's number is often rounded to $6.02 \times 10^{23}$.
e: True. Avogadro's number is often rounded to 6.02 x 10^23. Avogadro's number is about 6.02 x 10^23 particles in one mole. Avogadro links gas volume at the same T and P to the number of particles, and one mole holds 6.02 x 10^23 of them.

q: The mass of one mole of atoms of a pure element in grams is numerically equal to the atomic mass of that element in atomic mass units.
e: True. The mass of one mole of atoms of a pure element in grams is numerically equal to the atomic mass of that element in atomic mass units. One mole is the amount that holds as many particles as 12 g of carbon-12, which is 6.02 x 10^23 particles.

q: The mass of one mole of molecules of a compound in grams is numerically equal to the atomic mass of that compound.
e: False. The mass of one mole of atoms of a pure element in grams is numerically equal to the atomic mass of that element in atomic mass units. One mole is the amount that holds as many particles as 12 g of carbon-12, which is 6.02 x 10^23 particles. The mass of one mole of molecules of a compound in grams is numerically equal to the atomic mass of that compound.

q: The molar mass of an element or compound has units of gram per mole ($g \text{ mol}^{-1}$) or milligram per millimole ($mg \text{ mmol}^{-1}$).
e: True. The molar mass of an element or compound has units of gram per mole (g mol^-1) or milligram per millimole (mg mmol^-1). Molar mass is the mass of one mole of a substance, in grams per mole.

q: Hydrated salts are salts in which one or more water molecules are physically mixed.
e: False. Hydrated salts are salts in which one or less water molecules are physically mixed. A hydrated salt has water of crystallisation chemically bound in the crystal, not just mixed in.

q: The number of water molecules in hydrated salt can be determined by composition stoichiometry.
e: True. The number of water molecules in hydrated salt can be determined by composition stoichiometry. Stoichiometry is the quantitative bookkeeping of how much of each substance takes part in a reaction. Composition stoichiometry is about the quantitative ratios of elements inside a compound.

q: The water found in crystals is called water of crystallisation.
e: True. The water found in crystals is called water of crystallisation. Water of crystallisation is water locked into a crystal lattice in a definite ratio.

q: Water of crystallisation is defined as water that occurs as a constituent of crystalline substances in a definite stoichiometric ratio.
e: True. Water of crystallisation is defined as water that occurs as a constituent of crystalline substances in a definite stoichiometric ratio. Water of crystallisation is water locked into a crystal lattice in a definite ratio.

q: An example of a hydrated salt is copper(II) sulphate pentahydrate, $CuSO_4 \cdot 5H_2O$.
e: True. An example of a hydrated salt is copper(II) sulphate pentahydrate, CuSO_4 · 5H_2O. Copper(II) sulphate solution is a common electrolyte, and hydrated CuSO4·5H2O is blue. A hydrated salt has water of crystallisation chemically bound in the crystal, not just mixed in.

q: An example of a hydrated salt is oxalic acid dihydrate, $(COOH)_2 \cdot 2H_2O$.
e: True. An example of a hydrated salt is oxalic acid dihydrate, (COOH)_2 · 2H_2O. A hydrated salt has water of crystallisation chemically bound in the crystal, not just mixed in.
